summary.text: If \(n\) is Harshad, appending a zero gives the distinct partner \(10n\). Otherwise, with \(d=D(n)\), \(e=D(d)\), and \(a=(n-e)/9\), digit-sum congruences modulo \(9\) make \(a\) integral, while a finite check for \(10\le n<36\) and the bound \(2D(n)\le n\) thereafter give \(d<10^a\); then for \(c=a+\text{digits}(d)\), the number \(k=d(10^a-1)10^c+d\) is divisible by \(d\), differs from \(n\), and satisfies \(D(k)=e+D(10^a-d)+D(d-1)=e+9a=n\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(D(m)\) denote the sum of the base-10 digits of the nonnegative integer \(m\). A positive integer \(k\ne n\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\) when
\[
D(n)\mid k\qquad\text{and}\qquad D(k)\mid n.
\]
We prove that every positive integer \(n\) has such a partner. It then follows immediately that the sequence value \(a(n)\), defined to be the least positive partner when one exists and \(0\) otherwise, is never zero.

We first record the elementary facts about decimal digit sums that will be used.

1. If \(0\le B<10^r\) and \(A>0\), then
\[
D(B+10^rA)=D(B)+D(A). \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, the decimal expansion consists of the expansion of \(A\), followed by an \(r\)-digit block representing \(B\), with leading zeroes inserted into that block if necessary. Such zeroes do not change the digit sum.

In particular, appending a zero does not change digit sum:
\[
D(10m)=D(m). \tag{2}
\]
Also, for a one-digit number \(x\), \(D(x)=x\), and
\[
D(10^r-1)=9r, \tag{3}
\]
because \(10^r-1\) consists of \(r\) digits all equal to \(9\).

2. For every positive \(m\),
\[
1\le D(m)\le m. \tag{4}
\]
Positivity follows because the decimal expansion of a positive integer has at least one nonzero digit. For the upper bound, one may induct on the number of digits: writing \(m=10q+t\), where \(0\le t\le9\), gives \(D(m)=D(q)+t\le q+t\le10q+t=m\).

3. If \(m\ge36\), then
\[
2D(m)\le m. \tag{5}
\]
To see this, write \(m=10q+t\), with \(0\le t\le9\). Since \(m\ge36\), we have \(q\ge3\). Using (4),
\[
2D(m)=2D(q)+2t\le2q+18\le10q\le10q+t=m.
\]

4. For every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
9r<10^r. \tag{6}
\]
For \(r=0\) this is \(0<1\), and for \(r=1\) it is \(9<10\). For \(r\ge1\), an induction works: if \(9r<10^r\), then
\[
9(r+1)=9r+9<10^r+9<10\cdot10^r=10^{r+1},
\]
since \(10^r\ge10\).

5. We need the following decimal-complement identity. If
\[
1<d<10^r,
\]
then
\[
D(10^r-d)+D(d-1)=9r. \tag{7}
\]
Write \(d-1\) as an \(r\)-digit decimal block, allowing leading zeroes:
\[
d-1=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}x_i10^i,\qquad 0\le x_i\le9.
\]
Since \(10^r-1\) is the \(r\)-digit number consisting entirely of nines, subtraction involves no borrowing and
\[
10^r-d=(10^r-1)-(d-1)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}(9-x_i)10^i.
\]
Consequently,
\[
D(d-1)+D(10^r-d)
 =\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}x_i+\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}(9-x_i)
 =9r,
\]
which proves (7).

We now fix a positive integer \(n\), and put
\[
d=D(n).
\]
There are two principal cases.

**Case 1: \(d\mid n\).**

Take
\[
k=10n.
\]
Then \(k>0\), and \(k\ne n\) because \(n>0\). Moreover, \(d\mid k\), since \(d\mid n\), and by (2),
\[
D(k)=D(10n)=D(n)=d\mid n.
\]
Thus \(k\) is a partner of \(n\).

This case in particular handles all \(1\le n\le9\): there \(D(n)=n\), so the respective explicit partners are
\[
10,20,30,40,50,60,70,80,90.
\]

**Case 2: \(d\nmid n\).**

The preceding observation shows that this case necessarily has \(n\ge10\). Also,
\[
d>1. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, \(d>0\) by (4), while if \(d=1\), then \(d\mid n\), contrary to the hypothesis.

Let
\[
s=D(d).
\]
Every integer is congruent modulo \(9\) to its decimal digit sum, because \(10^i\equiv1\pmod9\). Hence
\[
n\equiv d\equiv s\pmod9. \tag{9}
\]
Furthermore, by (4), \(s\le d\le n\). In fact \(d<n\): equality \(d=n\) would imply \(d\mid n\). Thus
\[
s<n. \tag{10}
\]
It follows from (9) and (10) that there is a positive integer
\[
a=\frac{n-s}{9} \tag{11}
\]
satisfying
\[
9a=n-s. \tag{12}
\]

The key estimate is
\[
d<10^a. \tag{13}
\]
We prove this first for \(n\ge36\). By (5) and by \(s=D(d)\le d\),
\[
d+s\le2d=2D(n)\le n.
\]
Therefore
\[
d\le n-s=9a<10^a,
\]
where the strict final inequality is (6). This proves (13) when \(n\ge36\).

It remains to check \(10\le n<36\). We only need to consider those \(n\) for which \(D(n)\nmid n\), since the others belong to Case 1. The complete list of relevant values is shown below. In each row, \(d=D(n)\), \(s=D(d)\), and \(a=(n-s)/9\).
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
n&d&s&a&10^a\\ \hline
11&2&2&1&10\\
13&4&4&1&10\\
14&5&5&1&10\\
15&6&6&1&10\\
16&7&7&1&10\\
17&8&8&1&10\\
19&10&1&2&100\\
22&4&4&2&100\\
23&5&5&2&100\\
25&7&7&2&100\\
26&8&8&2&100\\
28&10&1&3&1000\\
29&11&2&3&1000\\
31&4&4&3&1000\\
32&5&5&3&1000\\
33&6&6&3&1000\\
34&7&7&3&1000\\
35&8&8&3&1000
\end{array}
\]
The displayed values directly give \(d<10^a\) in every row. Thus (13) holds in all cases.

Let \(\ell\) be the number of decimal digits of \(d\), and set
\[
c=a+\ell.
\]
Since \(d>0\), the definition of \(\ell\) gives
\[
d<10^\ell\le10^c. \tag{14}
\]
We now define
\[
k=d(10^a-1)10^c+d. \tag{15}
\]
We will prove that this is a partner of \(n\).

First, \(a>0\), so \(10^a-1>0\); together with \(d>0\), this shows \(k>0\). Factoring (15) gives
\[
k=d\bigl((10^a-1)10^c+1\bigr),
\]
so
\[
d=D(n)\mid k. \tag{16}
\]
Moreover, \(k\ne n\), because if \(k=n\), then (16) would give \(d\mid n\), contradicting the hypothesis of Case 2.

It remains to compute \(D(k)\). By (14), the final summand \(d\) in (15) occupies a block of fewer than \(c\) decimal places. Formula (1) therefore gives
\[
D(k)=D(d)+D\bigl(d(10^a-1)\bigr). \tag{17}
\]
The estimate (13) permits the elementary decomposition
\[
\begin{aligned}
d(10^a-1)
  &=d10^a-d\\
  &=(d-1)10^a+(10^a-d). \tag{18}
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(0<10^a-d<10^a\), and \(d-1>0\) by (8), so applying (1) to (18) yields
\[
D\bigl(d(10^a-1)\bigr)
 =D(d-1)+D(10^a-d).
\]
By the complement identity (7), this is \(9a\). Substitution into (17), followed by (12), now gives
\[
D(k)=D(d)+9a=s+(n-s)=n. \tag{19}
\]
Consequently
\[
D(k)=n\mid n. \tag{20}
\]
Equations (16) and (20), together with \(k>0\) and \(k\ne n\), show that \(k\) is a Harshad amicable partner of \(n\).

Thus every positive integer \(n\) has at least one positive Harshad amicable partner distinct from itself. The set of all such partners is therefore nonempty and, as a nonempty set of positive integers, has a least member. That least member is positive, so by the definition of the sequence, \(a(n)\ne0\) for every positive integer \(n\).
